title: Purity
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

The purity code — Iwu Ọcha

Cleanliness in Odiana is not housekeeping. It is doctrine, it is law, and it is the largest single thing the religion asks of anyone.

A person who keeps the temple clean and a person who keeps their heart clean are doing the same work in two places. Ọcha — clean, white, bright — is what the religion is for.

1 · Why cleanliness is doctrine

The Igbo sources already carry the principle, and Odiana takes it further than they do:

  • nso is a taboo, and its breach is not a crime but a defilement. A religion whose central wrong is

pollution is a religion in which cleanliness is the first discipline, not a decoration.

  • alu is abomination, and abomination is described as something done to the earth: "the face of Ana

cracks, and drought follows unless cleansed." Pollution and drought are the same event.

  • And the guilt is shared: "When someone commits nso, it affects the whole community." So a dirty

place is not a private failing — it is everyone's.

Odiana's addition, and it is the Shinto inheritance: the tradition cleanses after defilement; Odiana keeps clean so that defilement has nowhere to begin. That is a change of order — from repair to upkeep — and it is the single largest reform in this project.

2 · What is borrowed from Shinto, and what is Igbo

Borrowed from Shinto, and declared here rather than presented as Igbo:

| borrowed | is | |---|---| | cleanliness as standing doctrine | the shrine is kept clean always, not cleaned when it is soiled. The discipline is daily and unending | | the washing place at the threshold | a place at the entrance where hands and mouth are washed before entering — Shinto's temizuya | | shoes off | the ground of the temple is not walked on with outside dirt. This one is also Igbo — see §5 | | white and undyed cloth | the purity marker, in dress and in hangings. This one is also Igbo: akwa ọcha | | salt | thrown, sprinkled, used as a purifier. This one is also Igbo: nnu | | the boundary marked | a bound and marked edge to the sacred ground. This one is also Igbo: nzu and herbs mark boundaries | | renewal on a cycle | Shinto rebuilds on a fixed cycle; see temple.md |

Not borrowed: Shinto's theology, its kami, its mythology, its priesthood. Odiana takes the discipline of keeping and none of the religion. A Shinto term is never used as an Odiana term.

And the Igbo ground is stronger than it looks. The tradition already has: barefoot entry to shrines and ancestral lands; sweeping with a palm broom as a spiritual act — "not only a physical act of cleaning but also a spiritual practice"; Anyanwu Ututu, the early sun, called "the best form of spiritual hygiene and the greatest instrument for conducting morning rituals", taken facing east; water infused with nzu for floors and walls; and ogilisi and uziza burned for purification.

3 · The three states, and the fourth

| state | is | how it is read | |---|---|---| | ọcha | clean · white · clear · in good order | the ordinary and required state of everything belonging to the religion | | nso | set apart · taboo · not to be touched or done | a state to be kept, and its breach is defilement | | alu | defiled · abominable | a state to be repaired, and the repair is ikpu alu |

And the fourth thing, which Odiana adds: ọcha na-adịgide — cleanliness that continues. Not a state reached after a cleansing, but a state held. The temple is judged on its ordinary day, not on its festival day.

4 · The daily keeping

Every day, at every Ndose, in this order:

| # | what is done | why | |---|---|---| | 1 | the ground is swept — with a palm broom, at dawn, before anything else | sweeping is the religion's first act, and it is a rite: "the sweeping away of unwanted influences and the restoration of spiritual purity" | | 2 | the sweepings are taken away and burned or buried — never left at the edge of the ground | dirt removed and left at the threshold has not been removed | | 3 | the surfaces are wiped with clean water — the sill, the platform, the altar, the seats, the emblems | | | 4 | fresh water is set in the vessels | standing water is not clean water | | 5 | the court is raked or smoothed | the ground of the Ndose is an orderly surface, not a swept one | | 6 | the threshold is washed | the boundary between outside and inside is washed daily, and it is the part of the temple that is washed most | | 7 | the morning sun is taken — Anyanwu Ututu, facing east, before ten | "the best form of spiritual hygiene and the greatest instrument for conducting morning rituals" | | 8 | the offering is made — kola and water, and a libation | see liturgy.md |

At dusk: the offering again, the water vessels emptied and refilled, and the ground walked once to see that nothing has been left on it.

And the sweeping is not done by a servant. Every person who uses the Ndose sweeps it in turn — the Eze and the newest member alike. A religion whose cleanliness is doctrine cannot delegate it.

5 · The person

Before entering

Wash the hands and rinse the mouth at the washing place at the threshold, and take off the shoes. Both are required of everyone without exception.

Barefoot entry is the firmest rule in the code, and the best-attested: the shrine prohibitions of the Igbo sources place "wearing shoes" among the things forbidden in shrines and ancestral lands, barefoot practice is presupposed across the corpus, and it costs nothing, sheds nothing, and binds a child, a stranger and the Eze alike.

What is worn

White, or undyed, or clean. Akwa ọcha — white cloth — is the religion's own purity marker and not a borrowing. No footwear beyond the threshold. No dirt brought in on the body or the clothes.

And nothing that has been in contact with blood is worn into an Ndose — see §7. In a religion that kills nothing, this is easy to keep, and it is kept without exception.

The body's own keeping

  • hands washed before any offering, and after any contact with the dead, the sick, or waste;
  • the mouth rinsed — the tradition's own requirement, and it is why the washing place serves both;
  • the body clean, and the hair and nails kept;
  • no strong perfume or smoke carried into the Ndose, because the place of offering is not the place of

scent. Incense belongs to the offering, not to the person.

And the purity that is not physical

Anger, deceit, and a debt unpaid are defilements too, and Nchegharị — the confession — is their cleansing. A person who enters clean and carrying a lie has not entered clean. This is the one place where the code crosses from the ground to the person, and it is stated because a purity code that only counts dirt is a code for sweeping, not a religion.

6 · The temple's ground

| rule | is | |---|---| | the ground is swept daily | §4 | | the boundaries are marked with nzu or with planted herbs, and the marking is renewed | an unmarked sacred ground is not a sacred ground | | nothing is thrown or left inside the boundary | no rubbish, no sweepings, no broken vessel, no food | | no animal is kept, tied or slaughtered within the boundary | no animal is ever kept or tied inside the boundary, and none is killed within it — the animal of a festival is killed in the open, beyond it — see §7 | | no standing water is allowed anywhere in the ground | water is kept moving, emptied, and refilled; a vessel of still water is emptied at dusk | | the drains run clear, and are cleared whenever they do not | | | planted ground is kept planted, and bare ground is kept smooth | | | the path to the Ndose is kept clean — the approach is part of the temple | dirt on the road to the temple is dirt at the temple | | nothing is built or stored against the temple wall | | | the Ndose is not a store | what is not used in the religion is not kept in it |

And the rule that covers the whole of it, in the words of the author's own source: "Nothing used pollutes land or water." No rite in Odiana may leave the ground or the water worse than it found it.

7 · Blood

No blood is brought to an altar or a shrine in Odiana, and nothing holy is ever touched with it. But an animal is killed at the festivals of this religion and at its serious rites — in the open, beyond the shrine and away from every holy thing.

That is the religion's largest single reform, and this code is where it is most visible. Three consequences:

1. The altar is never a killing place, and there is no vessel for blood in an Ndose. 2. No person who has handled blood enters an Ndose until they have washed and changed. This is not a punishment; it is the same rule as shoes, at a greater scale. 3. The tradition's own bloodless offering is what Odiana offers to Chukwu and at its household shrines — and the tradition agrees, because it never offered blood to the supreme God at all: "Blood sacrifices are not offered to Chukwu… The type of offering made to Chukwu is one made up of kola nut, white chalk and libations of palm and raffia wine."

What Odiana does not claim. The tradition does not say that killing is wrong — one of its own texts calls bloodshed "not an act of violence but a sacred duty" — and its anti-blood doctrine is concentrated on human blood. Odiana's bloodless rule is a reform made by law (iwu), and every document that states it says so.

8 · Cleansing — ikpu alu

The repair, when the keeping has failed.

A cleansing is licensed. In the tradition, purification may be performed only by "specially authorized persons"; in Odiana only a priest licensed through the eze ana may cleanse. This is the one act that must never be done by an amateur, because a bad cleansing spreads what it was meant to remove.

The ordinary cleansing, for a person or a place

| # | what is done | |---|---| | 1 | the ground is cleared and the boundary re-marked with nzu | | 2 | water is poured — clean water, at the threshold and at the altar | | 3 | the surfaces are washed with water infused with nzu | | 4 | ogilisi or uziza is burned, and the smoke carried through the space | | 5 | white cloth is laid or hung | | 6 | the declaration is made by the priest, and answered by those present | | 7 | the water is taken away, and poured where it will not foul anything |

The greater cleansing, for an alu

The tradition grades this by what is given — a live he-goat, sixteen yams, and a ram's skull that is mandatory — and Odiana does not follow it, because it kills. What replaces it is recorded openly:

  • the same seven steps, performed by a licensed priest, with the community present;
  • the assembly's acknowledgement, because "it affects the whole community" — the wrong was done to

everybody, so everybody hears the repair;

  • restitution where a person was harmed, as the law requires;
  • and a period of keeping, during which the person or the place observes the daily discipline of §4

without exception.

This is an innovation and it is marked as one. There is no bloodless substitute in the sources for a major ikpu alu, and canon.md says so in its amendment register rather than implying otherwise.

9 · The environment

Odiana holds that the ground outside the temple is the temple's business.

  • Water is not fouled. No rite of Odiana uses anything that poisons a stream, a well or the rain's

path — "Nothing used pollutes land or water."

  • The land is not left worse. Nothing is buried that will not return to the soil; the tradition's own

burial code forbids metal, plastic and cement in a grave, and Odiana applies the same rule to everything it puts in the ground.

  • Fire is used, not scattered. What is burned is burned in a place made for it.
  • The approach to every Ndose is kept as the Ndose — the path, the yard, the water beside it.
  • And a member of Odiana cleans what is in front of them. Not as a duty assigned, but because the

religion's first act is sweeping. A member who walks past filth on the way to the temple has misread the religion.

10 · The keeping of the year

| when | what is done | |---|---| | daily | §4 — sweeping, wiping, water, the sun, the offering | | each Eke — the first day of the four-day week | the water vessels are emptied and scalded; the cloths are washed | | each new moon | the Ndose is cleaned from the roof down, and the boundary re-marked | | before any festival | the greater cleaning: the ground, the walls, the vessels, the cloths, the approach — and the Nzemabua announces it | | at Igu Aro, when the year is announced | the whole ground is renewed: surfaces re-smoothed, nzu reapplied, cloths replaced, and anything worn is taken away and not returned | | at the death of a member | the household keeps its own ground clean and the Ndose is not entered by the bereaved until the cleansing of §8 is done |

And the announced calendar is what makes this possible — the Nzemabua publishes the year, so the cleaning before a festival is a date everyone knows and not a local decision.

11 · Who may not serve

| who | may not | |---|---| | anyone who has handled blood, until washed and changed | enter | | anyone who has handled a corpse, for the period the priest sets | enter or serve | | anyone carrying an unresolved wrong against another member | serve at the altar until Nchegharị and restitution | | anyone who has not washed at the threshold | enter — no exception, including the Eze | | anyone wearing shoes past the threshold | enter | | anyone who has brought dirt, rubbish or an animal into the ground | serve until it is removed and the ground cleansed |

And no one is barred for being poor. The religion's law says "No citizen of Odiana may fall into destitution" — and a purity code that only the comfortable can keep would be a code for the comfortable. Water, a broom, white cloth and nzu are what the keeping costs, and the Ndose provides them.

12 · What Odiana adds, and declares

| rule | inherited / reformed / invented | |---|---| | sweeping as a rite, with a palm broom | inherited | | barefoot entry | inherited | | water, nzu, ogilisi/uziza, salt, white cloth | inherited | | boundaries marked with nzu | inherited | | the morning sun and the facing east | inherited | | the washing of hands and mouth before the offering | inherited | | the washing place at the threshold | borrowed from Shinto, and declared | | cleanliness as a standing standard rather than a repair | reformed — the largest change in this project | | the temple judged on its ordinary day | reformed | | the approach and the surrounding ground kept as the temple | reformed | | everyone sweeps, including the head | invented | | the bloodless substitution for a major ikpu alu | invented, and marked as such in canon.md |

The blood ruling, in one place

(The ruling is canon.md A11, and it is the same in every document of this religion.)

An animal is killed at every festival of Odiana and at every serious rite of it. The announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing.

And no blood is brought to a shrine, or to an altar, or to a sacred object, or to a tree that is held sacred. Nothing holy in this religion is ever touched with blood. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana and it is iwu — made, and published, and dated — and it is not a custom recovered from the ancestors.

What remains bloodless, and stays bloodless:

  • the offering to Chukwu — the tradition's own offering was kola, white chalk and libation, and it is kept;
  • the household shrine — the household oblation is kola, nzu, mmanya and water;
  • the temple altar — no blood is brought to it, ever;
  • the consecration of objects — no shrine, Ofo, Ikenga or medicine is made with blood (canon.md A6);
  • a reading of afa — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee.

And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. Where the old practice used a human being, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.
